title: Virtual Environments
text:
First, some vocab:

Python dependency: an external package that a script (or other package requires to run)
Executable: a script that can be read and run by your computer without additional compiling
Interpreter: an executable file that takes a .py script and actually runs it 
symlinks: pointers that lead to a file
PATH executable: the directory in which a computer can search for executables when the full path name isn’t given

title: Virtual Environments
section: Why not just install packages globally?
text:
Why not just install packages globally?

Dependency conflicts! Different projects need different versions of packages (and each package may need a specific version of its dependencies)

title: Virtual Environments
text:
Enter Virtual Environments…
Essentially, a subfolder specific to a single Python version containing all of the executables and packages needed for your project.
Two types we’ll cover today:

Python’s built-in environment manager: venv
uv, modern package installer built in Rust

title: Virtual Environments
text:
Pros of Venv

Built-in (no additional install)
Easy to use and conceptualize

Venv is used largely for dependency isolation.

title: Virtual Environments
section: What happens when you use venv?
text:
What happens when you use venv?
Activating a venv changes where your computer assumes your files are! Here’s what changes:

sys.prefix and sys.exec_prefix:


sys.prefix: path to platform-independent (OS-independent) Python packages
sys.exec_prefix: path to platform-dependent (OS-ndependent) Python packages

title: Virtual Environments
section: What happens when you use venv (cont.)
text:
What happens when you use venv (cont.)

PYTHONPATH:


tells Python where to look for modules (i.e., to go to venv sites-packaes NOT the base sites-packages)


PATH variable changes


modifies the PATH variable to include the virtual environment Python executable

In short: Python is told to STOP looking for exectuables, modules, and 3rd-party packages in the directory where base Python is installed. Instead, Python looks for files inside the virtual environment

title: Virtual Environments
text:
What does a “venv” include?

A typical virtual environment file setup
/bin: stores the python interpreter, pip, and activation symlinks
lib/sites-packages: directory where 3rd party packages are installed
/include directory where C headers for packages are stored
Configuration file: all details needed to configure the venv

title: Virtual Environments
text:
What about uv?

faster package installation than venv/pip install
more robust dependency handling
project initialization (will initialize a root directory, git repo, .gitignore, etc.)

title: Virtual Environments
text:
What does uv include?

A uv project file setup for a project called “rpcats”Here the .toml file is a configuration file!

title: Virtual Environments
text:
In conclusion…

always use some kind of virtual environment / project isolation method
use venv for “simple and dirty”
use uv for more complex projects that involve publishing or development

title: SDS316 Syllabus
text:
Prerequisites: SDS 270 or SDS 271 or CSC 210 or CSC/SDS 235 or by permission of the instructor
Meetings: Monday & Wednesday || 7:00 - 8:15pm || Bass 002
💡 Office hours, booking non-office hour time, etc You can also catch me for about 20 minutes after class on Wednesdays.


The United States criminal legal system is increasingly data-driven. Technologies like recidivism algorithms and predictive policing give the appearance of numerical objectivity. But, without sufficient context, we cannot understand how these technologies work or the data that they are using. This course introduces students to the theory and practice of handling data about the United States criminal legal system. Students will engage with this material through in-depth reading about the history of crime, policing, and incarceration; seminar discussions; research design; and large data-driven projects.



After completing this course, students will be able to:

Identify ethical concerns in the development and implementation of data-driven systems, specifically in the context of the criminal legal system

Identify the phases of the US criminal legal system, and several data-centric challenges within each

Design and execute a data-centered research project about the criminal legal system

Implement a data-driven dashboard to showcase their findings

Convey quantitative information in written, oral and graphical forms of communication to both technical and nontechnical audiences (an SDS learning objective)

title: SDS316 Syllabus
text:
Participation and Classroom Expectations
When we have classroom discussions, we’ll be covering material that may have impacted our lives or our communities. It is impossible to separate our lived experience from our academic work, and indeed our expertise and knowledge lies within our experiences. That’s an academic way of saying – bring your whole self to class with you because it’s who you are and because it makes you a better student and researcher. When everyone is bringing their whole selves to class, there is likely to be disagreement, conflict, or at least some discomfort. During the first week of class, we’ll set some norms together that work for our group.
I expect that you will come to class prepared to participate, and willing to participate in ways that are both familiar and unfamiliar to you.

Names and Personal Pronouns
I affirm all forms of gender expression and identities. If you prefer to be called a different name than what is on the class roster, please let me know. Feel free to correct me on your gender pronoun, if you don’t use any pronouns, or if your pronouns change during the semester. If you have any questions or concerns about being addressed respectfully, please do not hesitate to contact me. For more information, see Smith’s page about gender identity and expression.


Time Commitment and Labor Expectations
This course requires a weekly time commitment. On an average week, you’ll spend about 10-12 hours total on this course (this is also a federal requirement for universities!). In a typical week, you’ll spend 2.5 in class, about 3 hours doing reading, and an average of 4-6 hours working on class projects. The distribution of this time will shift over the course of the semester with some weeks having mostly reading work and others having mostly hands-on development work.


Office Hours
My office hours are listed in the document linked from the syllabus, and I strongly encourage each of you to use them. Studies have shown (e.g. Henry, 2014) that some students do not take advantage of office hours or are otherwise afraid to “bother” faculty. When I was an undergraduate student, the first in my family to go to college, I never went to office hours and I really missed out. This paragraph is my formal invitation to you to come to as many office hours as are helpful to you. Holding these hours is a literal part of my job – and I like my job – so please use all of the resources available to you, including my office hours.

title: SDS316 Syllabus
text:
Course Policies

Code of Conduct and Interpersonal Safety
It is important to me to create a classroom environment where everyone can be successful. We will work together to develop a classroom code of conduct that works for the group that we will become this semester, and we will check in about it regularly. At a minimum, this code of conduct will include:

respecting and affirming the identities and lived experiences of everyone in the classroom

moving slowly when difficult content is presented

during disagreements, disagreeing with the idea and not the person

assuming positive intent when someone makes a mistake

honoring those who speak up about something that doesn’t feel good

This class has an unconditional timeout policy, which means that any person can call a time out for any reason. When someone calls a time out, we will thank them for being brave enough to assert their needs. My commitment to you is that I will:

work to acknowledge structural and interpersonal power imbalances
believe your accounts of your life and experiences
interrupt any harassing behavior

If you have any concerns or suggestions for how to make this class more inclusive, please reach out to me. If you’d rather do it anonymously, please leave a note in my faculty mailbox in Burton Hall.


Attendance
You are an adult and you can choose whether or not to attend class. Except in exceptional circumstances, I don’t provide summaries of missed material for students who miss class; students who miss class will need to get course materials from a classmate.
If you are sick, please don’t come to class! In general, the SDS department has a no-remote-attendance policy. However, we live in community here, and staying home from class when you’re sick is a way of caring for your Smith community. In these cases, you are welcome to contact a classmate to zoom you into class. I will not set up zoom for you when you are sick. Students should reach out to their class dean in the event of an extended illness or emergency; they can help you to navigate these situations with your instructors. Consistent with the college’s policy on student academic standing, if you miss more than four weeks of class meetings, you are in danger of failing to earn credit for this course (receiving a grade of E).


Electronic Devices
This course combines seminar-style discussion and hands-on technical work.
During seminar conversations, I ask that you close your laptops, put away your phones and participate in class discussion. Of course, there may be times when you need to take a call or send a message. In these cases, please step out of class to do so – do not use your device under the table, out of respect for your classmates. The is no exception to this policy other than an ARC accommodation.
During lab work, I expect you to come to class with a working development environment – there will not be time to troubleshoot your machine in class. If you need help, please come to office hours.


AI Policy
This Fall 2026 edition of the class will have a pedagogical partner who will join us to think about if and how we use AI in this class. The policy is one we will develop together. However, there are some guideliness that will hold regardless of the outcome of that partnership:

you may not use AI to generate ideas. AI is not an idea generation machine, it is a probablistic language predictor. As a result, any idea that AI generates is one that many people have had before.

you may not use AI to generate writing or to edit/proofread something that you wrote. I would rather read your worst writing on your worst day than a single sentence generated by AI. Communicating complex ideas of the key skills that we practice in this class and AI cannot help you develop that skill, unfortunately.

I’m currently researching partisan gerrymandering and helping a professor in the mathematics department develop a new baseline against which to judge fair redistricting, with a focus on preserving minority-majority districts. I’ve been interested in this topic since I discovered Dr. Wes Pedgen’s research using Markov Chain Monte Carlo for redistricting, as it was the first time I really understood that my passions for math, computers, and government/political science could intersect. Since then, I’ve followed the work of Moon Duchin, who works out of UChicago’s Data and Democracy lab on some of the more advanced models for fair redistricting. Broader Relevance
Write about 100 words discussing why you think the answers to these questions might matter to others. Is this an understudied topic? Have the conclusions you’ve been seeing about it been wrong or missing something? This is your answer to the “so what?” question
Gerrymandering is a topic that has gotten an increasingly large amount of attention in recent years; however, it appears that academic research on prison gerrymandering has not kept pace, with most well-cited articles on the topic dating back at least four years, if not more. This is unfortunate since prison gerrymandering, just like other kinds of gerrymandering, disproportionately impacts black and brown voters and shifts power from urban centers to rural areas. These effects compound the existing voter suppression and disengagement that is prevalent in communities with high incarceration rates. Prison gerrymandering also violates the “One person, one vote” tenet. In one region, a representative won with just two write-in votes (one of whom was his wife) because only 58 of the over 1300 individuals assigned to his district were part of the non-incarcerated and therefore eligible voting population. The Census Bureau is aware of prison gerrymandering as a pressing issue, as, during the 2020 census process, over 77,000 comments were submitted asking it to reconsider the way it assigns imprisoned individuals to home addresses, with only 4 comments advocating for the current allocation scheme. So this is clearly a topic on which the public has an opinion, yet academic research and government action lag behind.

Personal Motivation
I’m interested in this topic because it’s questions that have come up to me as I’ve seen the way children are treated in the media when it comes to ‘crime’ commiting. In particular, I’ve noticed that young school shooters are often treated on social media as derserving of harsh, adult-like sentences. Just recently, I saw the Apalachee High School school shooter who was only 16, sentenced to life without parole. My dad’s best friend was charged as an adult at 17 to almost 7 years for a crime he commited, and it makes me wonder why he was treated as so. Was it because of the crime he committed? Or because he was a black teenager? Why was his sentence so long if it was his first offense? This made me want to investigate this discrepancy we often see today in how children are treated in the criminal justice system.

title: Research Plan
text:
Relevant Literature
TBD Interview Answers: I don’t have this data yet, but I plan to ask my father’s friend about his experience being charged as an adult and how that has impacted his life, his sense of identity, etc, and use that in my research. This can help in my third research questions focusing on how children put into the criminal justice system view themselves
I Was A Child In An Adult Prison System. Now I Fight For Those, Like Me, Who Deserve A Brighter Future When They’re Released: Catherine Jones was charged with second degree murder at 13 and spent over 16 years in Florida’s adult prison system. She describes how she was instantly relabeled a “super predator” and “killer” rather than a child, which speaks to Research Question 1 (where the line between child and adult is drawn) and how the public frames young offenders. She also says that her abuse went unheeded by adults she told, that prison programming was withheld from people serving long sentences, and that employers turned her away after release, all of which show the impacts of being charged to long sentences as a child (question 3).
Children Charged as Adults in Justice System Have Overwhelming Histories of Trauma, Researchers Find: The Imprint interview (Sara Tiano’s Q&A with researcher Aiden Lesley) summarizes a Human Rights for Kids survey of more than 2,200 people incarcerated for crimes committed as minors, finding that 94 percent experienced multiple childhood traumas and that this history was considered in court in only about 10 percent of cases. That speaks to Question 1, because it shows the “adult” label is applied without weighing the developmental and trauma factors that distinguish children. This interview also gives some insight into some of the harsh experiences children face once in prison (abuse risk, solitary confinement, etc)
Youth Confinement: The Whole Pie 2025: Using 2022 juvenile court data, the report finds that Black youth were 37% of delinquency cases but 59% of judicial transfers to adult court, while white youth were 43% of cases and 26% of transfers, and that the disproportion has worsened since 2005. It also cites Florida data showing prosecutors direct-file Black boys at seven times the rate of white or Latino boys, and its footnotes speak to Question 1: four states (Georgia, Louisiana, Texas, and Wisconsin) automatically prosecute 17 year olds as adults, and 22 states plus DC had at least one transfer provision with no minimum age as of 2019. The report also discusses adultification and the “super predator” myth, which ties back to my potential question 4
Most children charged as adults in Washington are youth of color: Henshaw reports that in 2023, 83% of Washington children charged as adults were not white, and that disparities appear both where state law mandates adult charging and where prosecutors have discretion. A 2024 University of Washington report found that of 28 cases where a white child was charged with first or second degree assault with a deadly weapon, none went to adult court, compared with 28% of similar cases involving Black and Latino youth. The article also ties this to adultification, with lawmakers pointing to language in court documents. This all touches on my research questions 1,2, and 4
A New Juvenile Justice System: Total Reform for a Broken System: Henning argues that prosecutors, who hold the most discretion over whether a youth is charged, are influenced by racial stereotypes about maturity and dangerousness. She cites studies showing that race shifts how culpable, mature, and deserving of harsh punishment a young offender is judged to be, even though self report data show adolescents of all races engage in similar risk taking. This connects to my questions 1 and 2 of who draws this line and the factors that influence whether a child is treated as an adult
Off Balance: Youth, Race & Crime in the News: This is a study focused on answering the questions: (1) does news coverage reflect actual crime trends, (2) how does news coverage depict minorities and crime, and (3) does news coverage disproportionately depict youth of color as perpetrators of crime? This connects to my research question 2 about factors that influence how children are treated in the criminal justice system, as well as my potential question 4 about how media/public narratives about young offenders differ by race and type of crime
Girlhood Interrupted: The Erasure of Black Girls’ Childhood: the report finds that adults in a survey saw Black girls as more adult-like and less in need of protection and nurturing than white girls, starting as early as age 5, and it links that “adultification” to harsher discipline in schools and the juvenile system. That speaks to where the line between child and adult gets drawn, and it covers both race and gender, two of the factors in my research question 2. This also touches on my potential 4th question
The Essence of Innocence: Consequences of Dehumanizing Black Children: Goff and colleagues ran a series of studies showing that Black boys are seen as older and less innocent than white boys, and that this perception carried over to how much culpability people assigned them. The authors also found that police officers who held dehumanizing associations toward Black people were more likely to have used force against Black children in custody. This strongly connects to my second research question as well as my potential 4th question
Race and the Fragility of the Legal Distinction between Juveniles and Adults: Rattan et al. surveyed 735 White Americans (658 in the final sample), and changing a single word in a case description, from “white” to “black” male, made participants see juveniles in general as more similar to adults in blameworthiness and more supportive of life without parole. This connects to my research questions 1 and 2 and my potential question 4 about how perceptions relate to sentencing expectations

title: Research Plan
text:
Relevant Literature

Noncitizen Justice: The Criminal Case Processing of Non-US Citizens in Texas and California This article uses court records from Texas and California (2005-2019) to show how charging, pleabargains, and sentence lengths differ for immigrants (undocumented people, lawful permanent residents, and visa holders). The model used in the article give me an overview of people’s status in two of the very highly populated states.
Law-Abiding Immigrants: The Incarceration Gap between Immigrants and the US-Born, 1870–2020

The source documented immigrant–native incarceration gaps and include detailed figures for 2000-2020,using census micro-data and prison rosters. The data for the 2000–2020 period overlaps with my timeframe I’m aiming for. I see it as a research I can try to build apon.

Immigrants are not criminals: Respectability, immigration reform, and hyperincarceration he article argues that the “good immigrant / bad immigrant” storyline has steered lawmakers toward policies that cage non-citizens far more often than the actual crime data would warrant. That lens helps me read my own numbers. If my results show longer sentences or more pre-trial jail time for non-citizens, this piece offers an explanation (stigma and policy design).
TRAC Immigration This source provides annual data on ICE detention figures, lengths of stay, and transfer sources from the year 2000 onwards. I can connect this with state prison or federal sentencing data to estimate exactly how much longer non-citizens were detained due to the “criminal-to-immigration” pipeline.
A day in the life of a 19-year-old in ICE detention: ‘I feel that this nightmare is not going to end’ The report tells an undocumented minor who was transferred from a county detention facility to ICE custody, only to face indefinite detention. The article clearly explains the process of “dual detention” for the same case. It inspire me to consider the issues of transparency regarding detention reviews in the post-pandemic era.
Letters From Detention The website collects hundreds of handwritten letters from detained immigrants, covering topics such as pending transfers, denied bail, and the hardships faced by their families. These letters make me understand more the lived experiences behind the “extra days of detention” figures in the data tables.
Citizenship and Punishment: The Salience of National Membership in U.S. Criminal Courts The author calculated that non-citizens receive sentences averaging 4–11% longer than those of citizens. It concluded that ‘Noncitizens face harsher U.S. prison sentences compared to citizens’. This article presents standard control variables and models, I can maybe try adopt this framework.
Disparities in the Pretrial Process: Race, Ethnicity, and Citizenship Research shows that non-citizens face greater difficulty obtaining bail and endure longer periods awaiting trial, meaning the disparity begins to accumulate well before sentencing. This makes me realize that the disadvantage is not merely compounded at the sentencing stage. It let me think more about my analysis of total detention duration.
Federally Sentenced Non-U.S. Citizens by United States Sentencing Commission This show tells me, officially, exactly how many non-citizens were sentenced by federal courts, which offenses were most common, and the average sentence lengths. I can compare it against the trends I’ve mapped out for the 2000–2026 period to check for any discrepancies.
What Happens if an Undocumented Immigrant is Facing a DUI Charge? The article breaks down the entire process—from an undocumented person’s arrest for drunk driving to the issuance of an ICE detainer—into clear steps, while also highlighting specific pain points such as exorbitant bail and prolonged detention. It gave me insight into the practical realities of how immigration status affects the handling of misdemeanor cases.

Throughout the three CMS schools that I attended, it became clear that several inequities existed. title: Research Plan
text:
Broader Relevance
The school to prison pipeline is a relatively well known systemic phenomenon. This concept has numerous contributing factors with many interconnected parts. Looking at the relationship that this concept has with geographic and segregated matters is of extreme importance. CMS provides an important case as the district moved from a nationally recognized court-ordered desegregation to substantially greater racial and socioeconomic segregation following changes in school assignment policy. Some research has been done surrounding this issue, but the spatial overlap between school and neighborhood segregation and youth involvement in the criminal legal system is less studied. I hope to bring light to these issues by examining the geographic disparities that continue to persist to this day.

Stage #1 Reflection
The overarching theme of our group is the cause and effect of prisons and their geography. Collectively we took an interest in things such as gerrymandering, regional differences, how the location of correctional facilities impact the surrounding area, and how geography impacts the school environments of young adults. Across Rae and Jessie’s work rural towns and economies are especially relevant; prison gerrymandering typically shifts representation from urban areas to rural settings, which is due to the placement of prisons in primarily rural areas; such placement is within the scope of Jessie’s investigation. Hayden and Kayla both plan to look at how geographical differences can impact how individuals interact with the legal system. In short, Jessie will investigate why a prison is placed where it is, Rae will look at the state and national political implications of that placement, Hayden will explore how school/neighborhood segregation impacts juveniles, and Kayla narrows that down into examining the effects on how, specifically, Black individuals are treated within the legal system through regional differences.
We’ve started to compile a list of relevant pieces of literature to our topics and have already started to see certain overlaps. We’re hoping that these similarities will also be helpful when it comes to looking for datasets. Kayla and Hayden are both taking a comparative approach by looking at regional differences. While Hayden is looking at a smaller scale of just Mecklenburg County and Kalya at the general “North” and “South”, the overlap in investigating how a person’s place can impact their outcomes will be a shared theme. One general theme will be the idea of representation, which is a highly social concept, with far reaching societal impacts, so we hope that we can all help capture this more humanistic side together. Rae and Jessie may both rely on datasets relating to the geographic location of correctional facilities. Hayden and Rae will also likely both be looking at how people are geographically dispersed both demographically and socioeconomically. We all hope that we can use this research cluster as a way to bounce ideas off of each other despite there being differences between our projects. Having a general idea of what each of us is working on will be helpful as we’ll be able to see how each other’s projects progress and the background that surrounds them.

title: Ensemble analysis of prison gerrymandering refroms
text: Current methods in detecting partisan gerrymandering revolve around the use of ensemble models, which sample from the universe of possible legal maps in order to better understand the distribution of these maps and whether proposed maps are within the range of possibility if no partisan intent is assumed. However, ensembles are rarely used in any studies of prison gerrymandering and its effect, and I wonder whether ensembles, specifically Dr. Moon Duchin’s Recombination (ReCom) or Reversible Recombination models (RevReCom), have untapped utility in this context. First, I intend to examine whether the distribution of Democratic seats won across possible legal maps in Texas changes measurably after the reallocation of incarcerated Texans to their last known home address. Second, I’m interested in not only quantifying the impact of reallocation on the possible realm of maps, but investigating a way to use pre-allocation ensembles to detect the presence of prison gerrymandering. I choose to focus on Texas due to its relevance in the literature.
